content: The British Medical Journal (BMJ) is one of the most widely read and respected peer-reviewed general medical journals globally. It is published by the BMJ Publishing Group Ltd, which is owned by the British Medical Association. The group also publishes other notable specialty journals, such as The Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry, Heart, and Thorax, as well as Student BMJ, which is targeted at medical students worldwide. Initially named The British Medical Journal, the title was officially shortened to BMJ in 1988. The current editor of BMJ is Fiona Godlee, who succeeded Richard Smith after his resignation in July 2004. Godlee was appointed in February 2005, with Kamran Abbasi serving as the interim editor during the transition. BMJ is a strong proponent of evidence-based medicine and publishes a variety of content, including original research, clinical reviews, news, editorials, personal perspectives, and career-focused articles. In recent years, the journal has seen an increase in articles addressing medical ethics and healthcare in developing nations. BMJ also releases themed issues annually, focusing on specific topics such as Health in Africa, Management of Chronic Diseases, and Global Voices on the AIDS Catastrophe. Additionally, a special Christmas Issue is published every year on the Friday before Christmas. BMJ is available in four print editions, each tailored to different audiences but containing the same core content. These editions include the General Practice edition for general practitioners, the Clinical Research edition for hospital doctors, the International edition for overseas subscribers, and the Compact edition for retired members of the British Medical Association. Some international editions are also available in local languages. Manuscripts are submitted to BMJ through an online system called BenchPress, a service provided by Stanford University's HighWire Press. This system has been well-received by authors for its efficiency, eliminating many of the cumbersome procedures associated with manuscript submission in other journals. BMJ employs an open peer-review system, where authors are informed of the identities of their reviewers. Approximately half of the original articles are rejected after in-house review, and the acceptance rate for original research articles is less than 7%. Manuscripts selected for peer review are evaluated by external experts, who assess their importance and suitability for publication. Final decisions are made by the editorial committee. For manuscripts sent for external review, decisions are typically reached within eight weeks, while those not sent for external review are decided upon within two weeks. BMJ was first published in 1840 under the title The Provincial Medical and Surgical Journal. It quickly gained recognition for its high-impact original research articles and unique case reports. The journal's first editor was Andrew Wynter. Historically, its primary competitor was The Lancet, another UK-based journal. However, with increasing globalization, BMJ now faces competition from other leading medical journals, such as The New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) and JAMA. BMJ is considered one of the core general medical journals, alongside NEJM, JAMA, and The Lancet. Some experts also include The Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ) and Annals of Internal Medicine in this category, although these are biweekly publications. In 2005, BMJ was ranked sixth among general medicine journals. The journal has been a vocal critic of the misuse of impact factors, particularly their growing use in awarding grants and recruiting researchers by academic institutions. BMJ transitioned to an online format in 1995 and has archived all issues dating back to 1994 on its website. In addition to its print content, the website offers supplementary material for original research articles, additional news stories, and electronic letters to the editors. The BMJ website is notable for its policy of publishing most e-letters, referred to as Rapid Responses, in a format resembling a moderated internet forum. However, concerns have been raised about potential misuse of this feature by correspondents who may not contribute substantively to discussions. To address this, some British doctors developed a kill file filter using Greasemonkey to suppress certain commenters. From 1999, all BMJ content was freely available online, but this changed in 2006 with the introduction of a subscription model. Original research articles remain freely accessible, but other content, such as clinical reviews and editorials, now requires a subscription. Access restrictions are lifted one year after publication. BMJ, like NEJM, provides free access to visitors from economically disadvantaged countries without requiring registration or login. The Journal of Clinical Investigation (JCI), while not a general medical journal, is another notable biomedical research journal that offers its entire archive (dating back to 1924) freely online. In 2004, The Guardian Online recognized the BMJ website as one of the five most useful health sites on the internet.
